Menagerie

muh-NAJ-uh-ree -- from French menagerie, 'housing for animals,' from menage, 'household,' ultimately from Latin mansio, 'a dwelling' (related to manere, 'to remain, stay'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Menagerie is a zoo or varied mixture of things.

The retired circus owner kept a small menagerie of aging lions and one very opinionated camel in his backyard.

Worked Example

A wealthy collector's mansion turns out to house not just paintings, but also a pair of peacocks, several tortoises, and a llama that wanders the halls.

That odd, varied collection of animals kept together in one place is exactly what a menagerie is -- whether in a private home or a formal zoo.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

assortment: An assortment is any varied collection at all -- candies in a tin, tools in a drawer, opinions around a table -- with nothing alive implied. A menagerie is literally a varied collection of animals kept together, and even its figurative uses keep that liveliness: a menagerie of houseguests practically squawks.

hodgepodge: A hodgepodge is a jumbled mix thrown together with no order at all -- furniture styles, leftover paint colors, half-finished ideas. A menagerie, even used figuratively, keeps a hint of the exhibit about it: a varied collection of living, colorful creatures or characters gathered in one place, odd but on display.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

solitude: the state of being entirely alone, with nothing else around

uniformity: the quality of being all the same, without variety

Where it sits · how grand the animal collection is — flock → menagerie → zoo

flock vs. menagerie: A flock is the humblest kind of animal-keeping -- sheep or geese, all of one kind, grazing a single field -- while a menagerie is a grander, more curious sight: many different animals gathered into one varied collection.

zoo vs. menagerie: Zoo is a more formal and larger-scale word than menagerie -- a zoo is typically a public institution built for a huge collection of animals, while a menagerie is often smaller and can even be a private, personal collection.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — menag

Root — menag: household (from French ménage, tracing back to Latin manere, 'to remain, dwell,' via mansio, 'a dwelling')

Suffix — -erie

Suffix — -erie: a place for, a collection of (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Menag ('household' — from French ménage, tracing back through Latin mansio, 'a dwelling,' to manere, 'to remain or stay') + -erie ('a place for, a collection of'): a menagerie was originally just the animals that 'stayed' as part of a household's grounds, before the word narrowed to mean a varied animal collection.

Use the root in a new word: mansion

Use the root in a new word: mansion: The old mansion at the end of the lane had been empty for nearly twenty years.

Word Choice

Menagerie most literally names a collection of live animals kept together, often privately or informally, but it's also used figuratively for any odd, varied mixture of things or people, as in 'a menagerie of mismatched furniture.'
